Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 223, to amend Part X of the Canada Shipping Act. He said:
This Bill has reference to formal investigations into shipping casualties. The law as it stands at present is contained in paragraph 781 of the Canada Shipping Act and subsequent sections. Under section 781, when a shipping casualty occurs, the

minister has the power to create a court of inquiry. Under that section he may appoint any officer in the service of the ' Government of Canada, any judge of the Superior Court of the province of Quebec, any judge of a county court, any local judge of vice-admiralty, or any stipendiary magistrate, for the purpose of making such inquiry. The provision is that the commissioner appointed for that purpose shall be a court. There are various subsequent paragraphs in the Act empowering the minister to appoint nautical assessors for the purpose of aiding the commissioner who may b.e so appointed in holding that inquiry. It will be seen, therefore, that with reference to inquiries into casualties the power of the minister is1 limited to appoint one commissioner, and that commissioner must be selected from a certain class of officials and judges in the country. In view of the appalling disaster near Father Point on, the 'St. Lawrence, and in consideration of certain communications which have taken place with respect to it with the home authorities, it is felt that in this case it is desirable that a special court of inquiry should be constituted, the finding of which would perhaps carry much greater weight and to which more importance would be attached than to the finding of an ordinary court of inquiry constituted under the provisions of section 781 of the Canada Shipping Act, which is the court of inquiry that has been hitherto established in all ordinary oases in which inquiry into shipping casualties has been thought desirable. The Bill which I am now introducing adds, as subsection 2 of section 871, the following:
In any case arising before or after the passage of this Act which the minister considers to be of extreme gravity and special importance, he may appoint two or more persons to be a commission to hold a formal investigation, and the commission so appointed shall for that purpose be a court, and such court shall, in addition to its judgment, make a full and detailed report to the minister upon the circumstances of the case, and may make such recommendations as may in its opinion be proper in the premises.
The words ' fit persons ' are the expression used in the Merchants Shipping Act. Under this subsection the power of the minister is not limited to any special class of persons, nor is it limited to the appointment of one commissioner. It is intended in the case of the late casualty to appoint a commission consisting of at least three persons, two of whom shall perhaps be
judges who have had wide experience in regard to admiralty matters. Consideration will also be given to the question of appointing as one member of that commission some one who shall be recommended by the British Government through the Colonial Office. Very great public attention has been attracted to the recent disaster in Great Britain, and it is felt by the Government that it is most desirable that the commission, constituted for the purpose of holding this investigation, should be of such a character as to commend itself to the judgment of all who are interested in shipping and navigation. I may say that this ship was registered in Great Britain, as in fact I think all the transatlantic passenger steamers are, with the exception, of those belonging to the Canadian Northern Company, which are registered in Toronto. There can Ibe no doubt, I think, as to our jurisdiction to hold an inquiry in Canada, because the disaster occurred in Dominion waters, even though the ship is on the British register. At the same time, I think it very desirable, if the Government of Great Britain desire to be represented on the commission appointed to hold the inquiry, that their desire should be complied with and that we should co-operate with them in every possible way in order to have the inquiry as thorough as it is possible to make it, so that the result of the finding shall be received with respect and may be of some benefit in the future.

On the explanation made by my hon. friend of the motives which have impelled him to bring down this Bill, I certainly am disposed to agree with him. Whether or not the enactment of the Bill will answer the purpose remains to be seen when we see the Bill in print. Up to the present time I have no fault to find; on the contrary, I commend the action taken by my hon. friend to have this awful calamity which has just befallen us investigated by the most ample, complete and searching inquiry by the highest possible authorities we can find. I am aware that we have in this country men competent to take part in this inquiry, but the suggestion of my hon. friend that the British Government should also be invited to take part in it and to select a commissioner is one which I think will commend itself to the judgment of the people, not only because the ship which has gone down is upon the British regis-

ter, but on account of the naturally superior knowledge and experience of men in Great Britain connected with shipping matters. We have within our own shores experienced and able men; but every one will agree that the experience of some of the British officers will be of great value in this inquiry. If the inquiry is to be based upon this Bill, the Bill ought to be passed into law as soon as possible, and on this side of the House we shall be very happy to facilitate its early passage.

In the Maritime
provinces, disasters have taken place and a great number of lives have been lost by reason of the fact that old and unseaworthy vessels have been imported into this country and that there have been no inspectors to inspect these vessels which should never have been allowed to go to sea. I understand that the inspectors of the Customs Department are required to pass them, but no careful investigation is made into the condition of the hulls of these vessels. Already this season several of these vessels have gone to the bottom without warning and valuable lives have been lost; and if there is no provision in the law whereby the hulls of these vessels may be inspected and the people who own them may be prevented from sending them to sea, this legislation affords the opportunity for providing for the appointment of inspectors for that purpose. The inspection would not cost very much. One man for the four Maritime provinces would not take two months in each year for this work, which would be of advantage to the shipping people and would save in one year the lives of a great number of people.

I desire to call the attention of the Prime Minister to a statement which appears in the Ottawa Evening Journal of to-day, as follows:
Mr. J. W. Black, rescued Ottawan, makes serious allegations against two officials-No Marconigrams until money was paid-Operator on Lady Evelyn, it is stated, refused to send message to relatives until charges were paid- Intercolonial railway ticket agent, it is stated, refused railway tickets to survivors.
Allegations of an important character are made by Mr. J. W. Black, one of the local survivors of the wreck, against government officials aboard the steamer Lady Evelyn, and the Intercolonial railway ticket agent at Rimouski.
Mr. Black alleges that the Marconi operators aboard the Lady Evelyn positively refused to send any survivors' despatches to relatives and friends without first being paid for them, and that the ticket agent at Rimouski station declined to issue any tickets without payment.
The former, he states, took from a Mrs. Green, of Toronto, one of the survivors, the last money she had in the world, a wet five dollar bill, to pay the cost of a Marconigram message to her relatives telling them she was safe.
* We were aboard the Lady Evelyn,' said Mr. Black, ' attired in our night clothes and I desired to send a message to my home in Scotland, and one to Mrs. Black's mother in Ottawa. I wrote them out and handed them to the Marconi official, who replied ' I cannot send these unless you pay for them.' Well. I replied, all that I have is the shirt I stand up in. Mr. B. Weinranch of Montreal, another survivor, stepped forward and pulled a ten dollar bill from a belt he had round his waist and paid the cost of my wires. Whether they were sent I do not know, but at all events my mother-in-law has not received hers yet.
I do not bring this to the attention of the Government with the view of blaming any member of the Government for this condition of affairs; but if these statements be true, the circumstances are so revolting as to be almost unbelievable. I merely desire to point out to the Prime Minister that if the regulations governing these officials are such that it is necessary for them to resort to such extreme measures as these, the Government should amend those regulations and adjust them along humanitarian lines.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The item to which my hon. friend directs the attention of the Government had not come to my attention. 
The allegations made are certainly worthy of investigation, and they will undoubtedly receive it.

As the paragraph read by my hon. friend refers to the Post Office Department boat, Lady Evelyn, I must say that I am very much surprised at the statements made, and I sincerely hope that they are not true. I received a report from the captain of the Lady Evelyn this morning in the shape of a night letter, which should be very satisfactory to the public, and which I have given to the press. He reports what he has done with his boat since this terrible disaster occurred, and I am sure that the country will appreciate the good work that he has done. Members of his crew took off their coats to give them to the people who were deprived of their clothing, and saved a number of lives. My hon. friend and the members of the House will see that telegram in the press this afternoon. In view of the good work they have done, it is hard to understand why the officers should have acted in this way. The names are not given, I see.
The name is given: Mr. Black, a resident of Ottawa, and one of the survivors.
The names of the officers, I meant.
It was the Marconi operator on the Lady Evelyn and the Intercolonial railway ticket agent at Rimouski.
I can only tell my hon. friend that this matter will at once be brought to the attention of Captain Pou-liot. If it is true, which I sincerely hope not, the matter will be promptly dealt with.

I agree with my hon. friend in hoping that it is not true. One can hardly imagine it to be possible. My only object in bringing this to the attention of the Government is because it is so at variance with the reports we have seen in the press in praise of the officials.

Mr. ROCHfE: That provision of our Immigration Act under, which a person who requests that inquiry be made into his case by a board of inquiry consisting of officials of the department, is entitled to receive the same.

I have not any details as to that. We have just received a wire to the effect that a demand has been made for a hoard of inquiry in each individual case. This, I presume, will cover one of the steps that the Government is taking to reject these people; if one fails, another will be called into requisition.
The minister said that ninety applicants have been rejected as being physically unfit for admission into Canada.
Yes.
How many have been examined so far, in addition to the number rejected and the number admitted?

I am not quite sure whether the medical examination, has been completed, but thus far ninety have been
rejected by the medical men, and thirteen have been admitted on the ground of former domicile in Canada.

Has the minister confidence in the report that is being made to him that ninety were properly rejected on the ground of physical unfitness, and that the only ones admitted were admitted upon the ground of former residence in Canada?

I have every confidence in our medical men out there; they are high up in their profession, and are experienced in this particular kind of work. Certainly, as head of the department, I have every confidence in their medical skill and their ability to carry out the law.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
subtopic: LETTER OF MR. J. McL. FRASER.
speechtext:
I beg to call your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the form of this question. It seems to come within the rule of the House which states that in asking a question no opinion shall be offered. This question makes the state-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

On the motion of Mr. White for Committee of Supply:

I wish to have a further word in regard to the movement of the Hindus now taking place at Vancouver. I have asked a number cf questions with regard to this matter, and I want to be understood that it is not with any intention or desire of embarrassing the Government in administering what is no doubt a difficult question and a delicate situation. I wish, however, that it shall be understood that so far as I am concerned I want my own position made definite and thoroughly understood, whatever may be the attitude of the Government. I am in hopes that the attitude of the Government will be in conformity with my view, but, if it is not, then, from my point of view, so much the worse for the Government.
The immigration law as it stands is a declaration on the part of this country that Canada is mistress of her own house and takes the authority and responsibility of deciding who shall be admitted to citizenship and the privileges and rights of citizenship within her borders. This I take it is not because of any declaration of individual or national superiority on the part of the people of Canada over the people of any other nation, country, or race. It is simply a declaration of an attempt to discharge a national, and, if you like, an imperial responsibility. We are in occupation of this country; we are in control of its affairs, and there is nothing that is of such intimate, immediate and ultimate, future concern as the character of the population that goes to make up the country. The country is the people; the people are the 
country, and it is the first duty of the country, as it is the first duty of the Government, to take such measures as may be right and expedient to prevent, if prevention is necessary, the occupation of this country by population that shall hamper and deter in any material degree the development of those ideals of civilization which we believe ourselves to be here for the purpose of working out to their highest degree. It was with that end in view that the immigration law at present upon the statute-book was placed there; and it is under these principles that, for my part, I desire to see this law administered.
In regard to the particular case that is now engaging the attention of the Immigration Department, as I said, I do not wish to hamper the Government by undue criticism; but in my judgment, the proclaimed attempt, the announced attempt on the part of these four hundred people from India to forte themselves into Canada in spite of the law, in spite of the policy of the Government of the country, is an occurrence that does not carry to the people concerned any special amount of consideration at the hands of either the Government or the people of Canada. It has been announced that this in an attempt to break down the policy of Canada as it has been hitherto' announced and enforced. The Government has the responsibility of preventing that breaking down from taking place.
Just as to how this matter is viewed by people who are in the empire, of the empire, and who have an imperial outlook, may I read a quotation from The Britannic Review? The writer says:
The able leaders of the Indian campaign, whenever they are at pains to explain and justify It in a broader aspect than that of a local quarrel in South Africa or British Columbia, present it as a movement which aims at nothing less than the complete equality of Indians with Europeans in all parts of the empire. That is an ideal which the Indian people are entitled to cherish, and it is to their credit that their leaders do so; even if it is based upon an inferior and impracticable conception of what * equality ' in the empire commonwealth means. It is not an ideal to which the little European communities, who are trying to hold for western civilization the empty lands which were won by enterprise of their British forefathers while Asia slept, can afford to make concessions of a kind involving the economic displacement of their own race.
Who is the writer of that?

I do not think the writer's name is given.
This is not a labour question; it is not a

racial question; it is a question of racial dominance and national existence. Under the plea of being fellow-citizens of the empire, the leaders of this movement, highly intelligent and wealthy men, have undertaken to assert an authority in the Dominion of Canada which shall direct its affairs, and to that extent control its destiny. When they have thrown out that challenge to Canada or, if you like, to the empire, there is only one thing to be done, namely, to meet the challenge halfway. This is not an ordinary instance of men coming to our shores looking for homes or an opportunity to labour. This is an organized movement for the purpose of establishing as a principle the right that the people of India, and not the people of Canada, shall have the say as to who shall be accepted as citizens of Canada. The fact that in their advocacy of the idea, the principle of world-wide empire is invoked, does not make it any the more true, the more possible or acceptable. My idea of world-wide empire is an empire in which each of its component parts shall be given and guaranteed the opportunity to work out the destiny of that particular part according to the ideals of the people and the material possibilities of that particular part. To say that we in Canada shall not be able to say who shall join us in the work of building up the country, that we must accept the dictation of other people as to who shall join in that work, places us in the position, not of a selfgoverning state in a free empire, but in the position of a subordinate dependency not in control of its own affairs.
I said I would not embarrass the Government by criticising, and I do not wish to do so; but I wish to say to the minister that in my humble judgment there has been a very considerable delay in dealing with this matter. These people came to Vancouver, I believe, nearly a week ago and it seems to me-I do not wish, I say to criticise, but merely suggest-that the greater promptitude that is used in dealing with the situation the less opportunity there will be for fault-finding from any side of the question. I have already questioned the Prime Minister and the Minister of the Interior as to whether or not they propose to take advantage of section 23 of the Immigration Act. I gather from the remarks of the Prime Minister that it is not the intention of the Government to do so.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What section is that?

It reads as follows:
No court, and no judge or officer thereof, shall have jurisdiction to review, quash, reverse, restrain or otherwise interfere with any proceedings, decision or order of- the minister or of any board of inquiry, or officer in charge, had, made or given under the authority and in accordance with the provisions of this Act relating to the detention or deportation of any rejected immigrant, passenger or other person, upon any ground whotsoever, unless such person is a Canadian citizen or has Canadian domicile.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend misunderstood me.

I am glad I did. I asked the question a number of times and in a number of different ways, and I understood from the Prime Minister that it was not the intention of the Government to take advantage of this .section but that it was the intention of the Government to permit the question as to the rights of these particular immigrants to be adjudicated by the courts.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend
misunderstood me and misunderstands me yet. The Government has no power to say to the court: You shall not issue a writ. If a writ issues which apparently is in contravention of section 23, the only thing the Government can do is to place before the judge the statute and say:	That prohibits
you from proceeding. It will be for the judge of the court to consider the statute in view of the circumstances disclosed and determine whether the court has or has not jurisdiction to proceed. That is the only way the Government can assert the provision to which I have alluded, as I understand the law.
That is not the way in which the Government has always asserted this provision, and it is not the way in which it was intended that the Government should assert its authority under the provision.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: What way was it intended?

It was intended that until the court of inquiry provided for by the Act had disposed of the immigrant's case no order of the court should be recognized. As a matter of fact, it excluded the immigrant from the jurisdiction of the court until he had been accepted or passed by the authority of the Department of the Interior. There was a case some months ago where some sixteen of these people came, a trial trip, I fancy, very much as this is a trial trip, asking admittance to Canada. The board of inquiry sat, and

they were rejected. But an order of the court was issued, and they were admitted on the decision of the court and not on the decision of the Department of the Interior. As a result of the success of these men in that case-as a direct result-this shipload of 400 were gathered up and brought to try the same thing again. It was a perfectly clear case that when it appeared that the Government was not able to shut the door, then means were to be taken to force it wider open. It was the slackness of the Government in the former case that is the occasion of this present attempt being made. Because they let in sixteen they should not have let in, they are faced with the necessity of either letting in or excluding 400. As I said, I have no desire to embarrass the Government in this matter, but I want it to be plainly understood that the responsibility of letting in or keeping out these people is up to the Government. They have the machinery, they have the means, and if these people come in it will be the fault of the Government-if fault there be-and the Government will have to take that responsibility.
The other, reason why I have taken the liberty of delaying the House to this extent is that if there is at the present time any shortage in the law, if there is any necessity for amendment in the law, the House is still in session, but it will rise in a few days; and I want to put beyond possibility the excuse the law is not sufficient to meet whatever purpose may be necessary, if the policy of the Government be, as I have suggested to the House, the policy which is embodied in the present Immigration Act, and the policy I would like to see carried out.

The hon. gentleman
blames the Government for undue delay in dealing with the cases of the Hindus because the vessel reached port a week ago. The Government do not plead guilty to any undue delay. We have been particularly careful in every step we 'have taken thus far. The hon. gentleman must recollect that the boat in the first place was at quarantine at Victoria for some time before proceeding to Vancouver. Since the vessel reached Vancouver these people have been undergoing a very critical medical examination. A good many of these, I understand, were troubled with diseases of the eye-trachoma and other diseases of that nature-and each individual had to be examined, and, being ex-

amined on board ship, it was a slower process than it would have been on land. We thought it better to take the precaution to have these examinations conducted on the vessel than to let these people land, as in that event we did not know what steps might be taken by their countrymen that might have caused a good deal of trouble to the immigration authorities. So as a necessary precaution we considered that the medical examination should be held on board ship.
The hon. gentleman states that it was because the Government did not enforce the law in the case of sixteen Hindus who were allowed into the country some time ago that we have this present difficulty. If there is any blame to toe laid for the admission of the sixteen Hindus into Canada that blame rests not on this Government, but on the Government in which the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) himself was Minister of the Interior.
It was because of the faulty nature of the Order in Council passed by himself, which Chief Justice Hunter ruled as unconstitutional and not in accordance with the statute, that those sixteen Hindus were admitted into Canada. This Government took steps at the earliest possible moment to remedy those faulty Orders in Council, and we consider that they will now withstand even the scrutiny of Chief Justice Hunter.
I quite agree with my hon. friend's suggestion that at this session, if anything could be done so to adjust the law as to carry out the wishes of Parliament and of the people, it might be desirable to do it. The officers of the Government are fulfilling their duties to the letter. We are examining these persons one by one. A board of inquiry is necessary in each individual case; this board of inquiry is starting work today.
The hon. gentleman seems to think that we have not been expediting the examination of the Hindus as we should have done, but I see no reason for finding fault with the Government on that score. It is better to be sure of our ground, better to conduct carefully and successfully those examinations than to have any reproach in the future against our officers for non-fulfilment of their duties. I quite agree with my hon. friend that our Immigration Act should be enforced; we desire to see that it is enforced without any undue harshness or severity. It must be recognized that those people being British subjects have, perhaps, more claim upon us than the average person com-

ing from an alien country. We do not desire to do anything that 'will be unduly harsh or that 'will grate upon their feelings, but at the same time we are taking steps under the provisions of the Immigration Act for self-protection; we are carrying out our own immigration laws to protect our own people. Some time ago it was drawn to our attention that the labour market in British Columbia was congested and that it was necessary to protect the labouring people, particularly in that province. In December, therefore, we passed an Order in Council for three months prohibiting the entry into Canada of labourers through ports along the British Columbia coast and the international boundary line. At the end. of the three months the Order in Council was extended for a further period of six months. This Order in Council refers not to Hindus particularly, but to labourers and artisans, skilled or unskilled, from any country and we are enforcing that Order in Council against those classes from all countries. I assure the hon. gentleman that every step has been taken that may be considered advisable or necessary to enforce the law. If in the future the law is found to be faulty, we will have to amend it. We have been able to [DOT]stop every gap by remedying the faulty Orders in Council that were passed by the previous Government, and we have amended them in accordance with the decision of Chief Justice Hunter and I do not see what under the circumstances we could otherwise have done.

I must express my regret that the discussion started by the hon. member for Edmonton should be taken up in the spirit just evidenced by the hon. Minister of the Interior. My hon. friend stated that be did not want to impede in any way with the action of the Government in respect of the admission of these fellow-subjects into our country; he said, on the contrary, that he wanted to support the 'Government in dealing with the matter in the right way. The aim of the Government, if it be in accordance with the wish of the people of British Columbia, should be to keep these intended immigrants from entering into Canada. This question, as has been stated by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, is one of broad consequences. We find that there is a condition im which one class of British subjects want to gain entrance into the country and another class 288
of British subjects do not want to let them in. The people of Canada want to have a white country, and certain o,f our fellow subjects who are not of the white race want to come into Canada and be admitted to all the rights of Canadian citizenship. They say: We are British subjects, as you are; we were born under the British flag; some of us have worn British uniforms; some of us have fought under the British flag; you should open your gates to us as you would if we were of the white race. There are other British subjects who say: we will not have them. What is the cause of this?
The question is not altogether a racial one:	the basis of the
objection is not wholly antipathy to the yellow races. When members of the Asiatic races go to South Africa, to the Straits Settlements, to British Columbia, to California, to Australia, or anywhere, the moment they come into contact with white labour and white workingmen, there is conflict. The reason is altogether an economic one. These men of the Asiatic races have been accustomed for ages to a standard of civilization entirely different from ours. They live more cheaply than we do; they accept a lower rate of wage. That is the commencement of trouole. So long as this is so, you will have the same trouble wherever Asiatics come into contact with men of the Caucasian race.
What is to be done? My hon. friend is trying to exclude them from this country. 1 know that if these Hindus are allowed to come into British Columbia, there may be riots on the streets of Vancouver and Victoria; that has happened, and may happen again. But the only way in which the difficulty is to be overcome is, so far as possible, by diplomacy; the law should be the last resort to be taken advantage of. We have an arrangement with the Japanese Government that has worked well. Last year my hon. friend the member for Vancouver (Mr. [DOT]Stevens) suggested that we should have some similar arrangement with the Chinese Government. I wish that we had some arrangement also with the Government of India. It would be well if the governments of China and India would undertake to do as has been done in the case of Japan; that is, restrain their own emigration. But, if a ship comes from India to this country carrying persons seeking admittance, and they are met by the law which says: You



are not to be admitted here; they -will go back to India with bitterness in their hearts, and the unity of the empire must suffer. These men have been taught by a certain school of politics that they are the equals of British subjects; unfortunately, they are brought face to face with the hard facts only when it is too late. In my humble judgment, while the Government will do well to keep them out, the best method is to resort, not to law, but, if possible, to diplomacy. Let arrangements be made with the Government of India whereby they will do as the Japanese Government have done: try to keep their own people at home. They may say: The white people come to our country; why should not the people of our country go to yours? That is logical, but, unfortunately, this is a matter in which such logic will not count; and we shall have trouble until the remedy which I venture humbly to submit is applied by this Government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My right hon. friend has spoken of diplomatic efforts which might be useful for the purpose of controlling immigration from India to Canada in the same way that our immigration from Japan is controlled. Doubtless he remembers that some effort of that kind was made under his Administration, and I think it was not very successful.
Quite the contrary.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think the right hon.
gentleman is mistaken. I am not aware that any particular success attended his efforts. Otherwise it would not have been necessary to have passed the Order in Council as to direct passage under the Act of 1910 which was promulgated upon the recommendation of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), then Minister of the Interior. The Order in Council which prohibited immigration from India, and indeed, immigration generally to the Pacific coast of Canada except by direct passage was undoubtedly invested with a certain significance, and that particular Order in Council would not have been necessary if the diplomatic efforts to which my right hon. friend alludes had had the success which he imagines.
We have not been unmindful of the considerations to which my right hon. friend alludes in that regard; but up to the present time I cannot say that any efforts along that line have been attended with the success which we certainly desired and

which might possibly have been expected. It is regrettable, as the hon. member for Edmonton has said, that this ship should have been despatched to this country when it was perfectly well known at the time she sailed that the Order in Council of December last was still in full force. That Order in Council had no special relation to the people of India or to the people of China or Japan. It had just as much application to labouring men and artisans from Australia or New Zealand who might seek to enter this country. It was not discriminatory in any sense against any race. It had and still has general application on the Pacific coast and also on the international border. It is greatly to be deplored that in the face of that Order in Council still in force under the legislative sanction of this Parliament this ship should have brought to our shores immigrants who cannot be admitted. I entirely concur in what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite that the laws of this country in that regard, and the regulations made under those laws, must have full force and effect and be carried out.
The only observation made by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior to which the right hon. the leader of the Opposition took exception, was in reply to certain blame which the hon. member for Edmonton attempted to cast on the Government ior the admission of sixteen Hindus last year. The Minister of the Interior replied to that by pointing out that these men came in by reason of the fact that there was a certain alleged defect relied upon by the chief justice of the province of British Columbia under which those men had to be admitted notwithstanding the Order in Council, for reasons adduced by the learned chief justice. That alleged defect in the Order in Council has since been made good. My hon. friend from Edmonton has alluded to section 23, and I pointed out that we have no power to direct the court as to what writ it shall or shall not issue, or as to the proceedings it shall authorize to be taken or otherwise. It is of course, conceivable that a court might issue a writ or make an order so absolutely in the face of section 23, that the officials of the Government, after the matter had been placed before the law officers of the Crown for consideration, might direct that the writ or order be disregarded under the expectation that it would be withdrawn by the court or reversed on appeal. That would have to be a very extreme case and a very plain case. Apart from that, the

only way in which the Government could assert the provisions of section 23 would be to point out its provisions to the court and ask the court in view of these provisions to take no action and to make no order. The hon. member for Edmonton will of course, remember that the provisions, of section 3 declare that the decision or order of the Minister or Board of Inquiry in order to secure the protection of that section must be made in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and a court might come to the conclusion-in fact, courts have sometimes come to the conclusion-that the particular proceedings which were attacked in the courts had not been begun or carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Act, and that therefore, the authority of that section could not be invoked. In the ordinary course it must be determined by the court whether a particular case is one in which the authority of that section can be invoked by the minister and his officers. It is intended to give very distinct protection, and it does give very distinct protection if the proceedings are under the authority of the law.

Before we proceed with these Estimates, I would like to refer to the purchase of a rifle range near Souris, P.E.I., for which fully three times the proper value has been paid. More than that, the opening of, this rifle range closes a public road which has been travelled for many years. If the Government proceeds with the closing of that road, I am informed that those who will be injured thereby intend to file a Bill of rights and claim damages against the Government. It would take me fifteen minutes to explain the matter as briefly as I can and it will not be worth while commencing the explanation now before one o'clock.
Go on.

No, I wish the
right hon. Prime Minister to be present to hear my statement of this case, because it is of some importance to the people affected by it. It involves a principle which is of considerable importance. This road was a matter in dispute between the man who sold the rifle range to the Government and those who had the use of 2881
the road. It was brought before the Supreme Court of the province and the Supreme Court decided that this road could not be closed. Now the Department of Militia and Defence and the Dominion Government are being made use of to close this road under these circumstances. It is a matter that the Prime Minister himself ought to take some notice of. I had! a question upon the Order Paper some time; ago asking the department if they were aware of the fact that by the opening of this rifle range they were closing a public highway, and the answer that was given by the minister was that they were closing no public highway. That showed me that the minister did not understand the situation. I wrote to the deputy minister last summer in regard to the matter and got no reply. My letter is on the file which I received. I also wrote to the minister and got no reply. My letter to the minister is not on the file. I want to bring the matter now to the attention of the committee in this public way and to ask that the necessary steps be taken to guard the rights of the people who will be affected by the opening of this rifle range. It is now one o'clock.

No, no.
Other hon. MEMBERS:	Carried, carried.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: The matter to which the hon. gentleman refers has been the subject of consideration by the department. There is no road whatever shown on the plan as submitted to us-no public highway; but any complaint that has been made, or may be made, will receive careful consideration.

My hon. friend from
Kings (Mr. J. J. Hughes) makes his statement that difficulties had arisen as to the existence of this road, that the matter had been in court, and that the Supreme Court of the province had decided that the road existed and that persons living in that portion of the country had a right to use It. Now, the contention is that the Militia Department have stepped in and by buying all this land for a rifle range have taken away from the people that which the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island says they have a right to. Perhaps after recess the minister will take up that view of it.

The Colonel's discoveries.-It is a fact long acknowledged by the cognoscenti that the creation of multitudinous honorary colonels is the greatest single military achievement accomplished by any country in any age. The people of Canada, therefore, could not have complained if Colonel Sam. Hughes had rested on his sword, in a properly becoming attitude and dpent the remainder of his official days in the humdrum contemplation of his achievements. But that is not the Colonel's way. His restless brain, teeming with ambitious energy, cannot be shackled. ' Give me problems or give me death,' it cries out; and since the world will not answer with a real war, the Colonel goes out to fight over again the historic battles of Europe and America. He has just come back from the States, and the American people will note with pride that he has found much to approve of in the generals who led their opposing armies in 1861. They did not do quite as well as the Colonel would have done, to be sure, but then, poor Grant had no honorory colonels to help him. Standing on a blood-stained field, with his honorary colonels and a newspaperman beside him, the Colonel could see the (blunders which the less-gifted general made; and, knowing all, he forgave all.
He was the more ready to forgive since, as it has been duly chronicled, he made two great discoveries beside which even the inspiration which created honorary colonels pales into insignificance. 'One,' we are told, 'was that war can no longer be regarded as a series of haphazard and ill-conducted conflicts,' but as something in which strategy and military tactics are to the fore. Every schoolboy knows the principles on which Hannibal, Caesar, Napoleon, Wellington and the others fought. Theirs not to reason why-theirs but to see a head and hit it. They had not heard of tactics and they
could not conceive strategy. Bluff, honest soldiers that they were, all they knew was that they had to fight. It is true they often won, but this was only because their opponents were even more ignorant than themselves. Had they met a single honorary colonel who had visited the battlefields of America, their fame would never have risen above the horizon. For he could not only have used ' strategy and tactics,' but he would also have learned (as we are told the Colonel did) that ' marksmanship is the essence of the military idea.' Those spoilt children of history used to imagine that the sight of their bows and arrows or rifles or cannons was enough to strike terror into the enemy and secure victors. Colonel Hughes proves the ridiculousness of that notion. He has discovered that the man who can hit the enemy he fires at is more dangerous than the man who can't. It is an overwhelming truth which should sink deep into every mind concerned for its country's defence. All the centuries have been waiting on its proclamation. There is not a military quidnunc in Europe who will not discuss it. But yesterday we were negligible as a military entity; to-day it is known that what we lack in numbers we supply in genius.
And one more bond has been forged between us and the great republic to the south, in that the lessons of its unhappy war have fertilized a genius which makes Napoleon look like a boy-scout.

Mr. Chairman, you have read history and you know that in 1861 a militia commission was appointed, and that it urged that the a dive militia of the country should be raised to 50,000 men with a reserve of an equal number. Galt, and, I believe, George Brown, prepared on that occasion a memorandum which has become historic and from which, with the permission of the committee, I will quote because it ^contains some homely truths which in my judgment should be repeated once in a while especially when we have at the head of the Militia Department an extreme militarist. Sir John A. Macdonald and his associates pointed out to the British Government that:

While fully recognizing the necessity, and while prepared to provide for such a system of defence as would restore confidence in our future at home and abroad, the best ultimate defence for British America was to be found in the increase of her population as rapidly as possible, and the husbanding of our resources to that end; and without claiming it as a right, we venture to suggest that by enabling us to throw open the Northest Territory to free settlement and by aiding us in enlarging our canals and prosecuting internal productive works, and by promoting an extensive plan of emigration from Europe into the unsettled portions of our domain, permanent security will be more quickly and economically achieved than by any other means.
The Council showed how this might be done without cost to the British exchequer, and how it might actually lighten the burden of defence about to be assumed by the people of Canada. They said the expenditure for militia had increased recently from $300,000 to $1,000,000 a year, and they agreed to train a militia force,
Provided the cost did not exceed the last-mentioned sum annually, while the question of confederation was pending.
With regard to the recommendations of the Duke of Newcastle the Council pointed out that the preceding Parliament had rejected the military commission's scheme as ' extremely disdainful to the country' not only on the ground that 'the method of enrolment was highly objectionable' but because it established military machinery
At variance with the habits and genius ot the Canadian people and entailing an expenditure' far in excess of the sum which the legislature and the people have declared themselves willing to provide.
They added that the rejection of the measure was the result
Not of party combination but of a deliberate conviction that its principle was unadapted to the occasion, obnoxious to the province and that the financial resources available for military purposes were unequal to the outlay.
In their opinion volunteer organization alone was suited to the country and there was 'a decided aversion to compulsory service '-the very compulsory service advocated by my hon. friend on many occasions, although he says he speaks for himself and not for the Government.

Moreover, 'the people of Canada are doing nothing to produce a rupture with the United States and having no knowledge of any intention on the part of Her Majesty's Government to pursue a policy from which so dire a calamity would proceed, are unwilling to impose upon themselves extra burthens. Let me quote again from the same memorandum. Referring to the Duke of Newcastle and his militarist views:
His Grace had expressed the opinion that by increased military preparations the credit of Canada would be improved, but the council contended that not the least important consideration was a due regard to the means at the command of the province, 'and that they hold that they are more likely to retain the confidence of European capitalists by carefully adjusting expenditure to income than by embarking in schemes beyond the available resources of the province. They are prepared to expend money on the Intercolonial railway and similar works, but they are not prepared to enter upon a lavish expenditure to build up a military system distasteful to the Canadian people, disproportionate to Canadian resources and not called for by any circumstances of what they at present have cognizance.'
This language has the same force and value to-day as it had in the days of yore when it was spoken by such a political giant as Sir John Macdonald. Since the House rose at six o'clock, I have looked up the report of the case in Prince Edward Island to which allusion has been made, and I find it reported in the Eastern Law Reporter, volume 4 (1908), McAulay versus McDonald. In 1907 or 1908 McAulay brought an action against McDonald in connection with the closing up of a right of way which the public claimed they had for many years travelled over down to the shore of the gulf of St. Lawrence, for the purpose of removing seaweed. McAulay put gates across the road.
Mr. SAM. HUGHES: Is McAulay the man from whom the Government bought?

Yes. McDonald tore
down the gates and passed through and went to the shore and got the seaweed. McAulay brought an action of trespass, and the ordinary pleadings took place. In his plea McDonald alleges that for many years he, with others of the public, exercised the right of travelling over this road, on foot, and with horses, carriages, sleighs, etc., to the seashore. That was tried before Mr. Justice Hodgson and a jury, and the jury found, as a matter of fact, that the public including McDonald had for more than forty years occupied this right of way as a matter of right. That judgment was appealed from to the Appeal Court of Prince Edward Island and the decision of that court was given on the 7th of February, 1908, the court comprising Chief Justice

Sullivan, Mr. Justice Fitzgerald and Mr. Justice Hodgson. They unanimously held that the finding of the jury was according to the evidence and refused to reverse the judgment of the trial court. They held that, as a matter of law, McDonald and all the public had a legal right to travel over that road. The minister can see that this would not appear in the registry office and if a search were made there it would not be found that the public had the right to pass over this piece of land. It is now alleged that the Militia Department is erecting a stop butt, which will have the effect of preventing the use by the public of that road, and I beg to read the following declaration on that point:
To whom it may concern:
This is to certify that the engineer who recently made a survey of the proposed rifle range at Norris Pond, Prince Edward Island, has staked and marked a * stop butt ', directly upon the present public road leading to the shore, and further that if the ' butt ' is built at the point at present indicated, it will positively close the road and prevent the public from using same, thus denying the people a privilege which they have enjoyed for many years.
The minister will understand that the legal right these people have is a right ot way; it is not like a public highway; it is only an easement over the land of Mc-Aulay. The public can use that portion of the land which they have used hitherto, and it may be only six or seven feet in width. With a stop butt on this easement, the public will be deprived of the right of getting to the shore, which is a very valuable right to people living in many parts of Prince Edward Island. I realize that as the Crown now owns the land on both sides of the road-
Mr. SAM. HUGHES:	That is on both
sides of this easement?

Yes. If the physical
conditions were such that the people could get down to the seashore at some other place, the minister might give them that right, but it is testified to, that this particular place is the only means of access to the shore. It is, without any doubt whatever, the intention of the people who are behind this scheme, to defeat the rights of these people which have been declared to them by the Appeal Court of Prince Edward Island, and when the minister comes to read all the facts in connection with the case and realizes who are the gentlemen interested, I think he will come to
the conclusion that a great big game has been put up on him. I hope it is not so bad that the minister may not be able to see some way out of it to protect the rights of these people. I find, in studying this case, that the counsel for the plaintiff McAulay are no less than A. L. Fraser, a former member of this House and a gentleman who was appointed by himself to be the appraiser of the value of the land, and J. A. Mathieson, K.C., the present Prime Minister of Prince Edward Island- I will exclude Mr. Mathieson because he may not have known of the later facts- but Mr. Fraser knew of the lawsuit, he knew of the decision of the courts, he knew that the public in 1908 obtained the legal right to travel over that right of way to the seashore, and he knows that if this stop butt is placed where these gentlemen allege it is to be placed, that he by his political influence is defeating the right which the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island gave to these people some five or six years ago. Not to say any more, it looks bad on the face of it. I will not say anything about the enormous price which the minister has paid for the property, further than to say I look upon the price as being an unimportant matter in comparison with the evident intention to defraud these people of their Tights. I am satisfied, from the papers and from the facts as we have them presented this afternoon, that the minister and probably the department would have no knowledge as to what was going on; but certainly the gentlemen in Prince Edward Island who have been advising the minister not only had a knowledge but have been acting with a degree of mala tides which I am glad to say w^e do not often find in the legal profession, because, as a rule, the legal profession does not play games of that kind. We win our cases if we can, but we do not attempt to go to the Government and get them to win our cases after the Supreme Court has decided against us. It is a case which the minister ought to look into, and one which I hope he will look into. The physical conditions of the country may be such that it is not possible to erect this stop butt in such a way as to give the people access to the seashore. The minister might change the line of fire, and thus leave an opening whereby the people of that portion of Prince Edward Island could get down to the seashore and exercise the right that they and their forefathers have exercised for generations.

I do not want to put on ' Hansard ' the comments that were made at the time in some of the Winnipeg newspapers. I want to say a few words in regard to technical education. Nobody can say that I have not always stated in this House that I was against militia expenditures. I said that in 1910, when the present Government were not in power, so no one can accuse me of partisanship. I am sorry that the Government have not acceded to the recommendation of the Technical Education Commission to appropriate $3,000,000 for technical education. I happen to know something about what technical education will do, for I have the honour to be a member of the Technical School Board of the city of Montreal, and I know what they have been able to accomplish with the little money that is placed at their disposal. The minister may believe the commission has done wrong, and that the boys can learn a little more in the militia than they can in the technical schools. The minister will, however, agree that he finds it very hard at the present time to induce young men to join the militia, because, judging by the manner in which he is operating all through the country in putting at the disposal of young men everything possible to induce them to join, it seems to me he has great difficulty in attracting them. I will tell the minister also that in the near future it will be much harder to get men. The minister may have in the militia a good many men, but I fail to see that they are what you would call real soldiers, for this reason, that, in the event of war, the great majority of them would not do much fighting.
Why?

Because they are not
used to hard knocks; they cannot fight. It takes another class of manhood altogether to fight. The minister has told us about the military expenditure of Germany,
France and England. If we were to ask the people of Canada to tax themselves for military purposes to the extent that is done in England, I believe the expenditure would have to be reduced, because if the people were called upon to pay directly what the minister wishes to expend, they would want him to spend much less. The minister referred to Germany. Of course, the military expenditure is very heavy there. But anybody who reads history and keeps in touch with economic conditions in European countries can plainly see that the last election in France had a great deal to do with military and naval matters. The same feeling prevails at the present time in Germany. Two yeaTS ago, when I spoke on the Budget. I advised the Government that they had better wait until January to see what Germany was going to do in the election. We have seen what happened at that election in Germany, and we have heard about the election lately, in France, and we see a peculiar condition. We shall probably see the same thing in England in the very near future. They are going to do away with spending so much money on military matters. Conditions in the United States are exactly similar now. The minister may not believe me; I do not ask him to believe me. I can tell him that I know what I am talking about, from the economic standpoint. There is a feeling of discontent growing steadily amongst thousands in other countries, and that feeling is growing in this country. If the minister would grant the Minister of Labour, for instance, the $3,000,000 that was asked for by the Technical Education Commission, I can tell him that it would do a great of good. There is one thing upon which the manufacturers and the industrial element will agree and it may be the only one; that is, in technical education, and it is a wonder that the Manufacturers' Association, who are very powerful with the present Government, have not seen fit to prevail upon the Government to vote a sum for technical education. The manufacturers themselves see the necessity of technical education, because, if we have good technical schools, they will not have to go abroad to find competent men. At the present time, we must admit that we have to go to France, Germany or Belgium to get technical men. We are doing nothing in that direction, and I do not know why nothing has been done this year.
The minister is expanding his department, and probably is increasing the Ted tape

Of course, everybody knows that I am against that. There is too much red tape, and there are too many officers who want to have braid on their clothes. At the same time, the soldier of industry is earning the money to pay for it-indirectly, to be sure. If we had a direct tax for militia, the minister would surely find out the answer of the masses of the people of the country. I am not speaking for the farmer, because there are others who can speak for him. I do not want to go into detail as to what the militia has done in the West, in Montreal, and in Valleyfield to keep 'peace and harmony ', as they say. I want to tell the minister that the mass of workingmen-he may say they do not amount to very much numerically. Well, they amount to more than he believes. I am not speaking only of organized labour. Organized labour, of course, represents a certain number of men in the country, and they are paying their share to the Militia Department's piper; but there are also all the other labouring men, who, though not directly affiliated, are in sympathy with them, and who are discontented with this large expenditure. When we see the amount of money we are asked to vote for the militia and consider the thousands of men who are idle in the country, we must admit that the amount asked for should show a reduction instead of an increase.
The minister will probably tell me that we have a very small number of regulars in the country. So much the better. Regulars are unproductive, and worth nothing at all to the country. I do not believe there will be war between Canada and any other country. At the congress between the workmen of England, France and Germany, it has been decided that before they will fight anywhere they will find out what they are fighting for, whether for the interests of the country ot for the interests of a few large private institutions.
I believe, Mr. Chairman, that the future not only of Canada but of the world is involved in this question. I shall probably have the. advantage of attending the congress to be held in England next September; I know that this question is going to be discussed and I will tell them exactly what I think. The minister says to-night that he is not going to take a back seat; he says, I am going to do this and I am going to do that. I give him credit for that; I would rather hear him express his views that way than beat about the bush and say that he is going to do something which he does not 
intend to do. It has been said time and again that the course taken by the Militia Department is all due to the minister; labouring men have said that it is the fault not of the Government but of the minister; that the Government is not behind the minister in the course which he has taken. But the minister told us very plainly this afternoon that it was not the minister but the Government who decided to do what the minister is doing, and that in the future they will increase as much as possible the expenditures in the Militia Department. I want to enter my protest in that regard; I do not believe it is fair. I believe that a certain amount of that ' money should be devoted not to this purpose but to the technical education which is so badly needed in this country. If that were done we would have better men and better institutions. It would please the Manufacturers' Association, perhaps; at any rate, it would please the masses of the workingmen far better.

Mr .'Chairman, before the estimates of the Department of Militia are passed, I wish to refer briefly to the matter of expenditure for militia purposes. I dealt with that subject last year, and I may be allowed to revert once more to it this year.
I listened attentively this afternoon to the remarks of the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie). Although I do not wholly agree with him in all his conclusions, I heartily concur in his condemnation of the extraordinary outlay which this Government is making fo.r militia purposes, as well as ifor the building of armouries. 'The latter are, to my mind, provided in too large numbers in the province of Ontario, and are at times built in small villages with a population of only 500 or 1,000 people. From the remotest point of the Gaspe -peninsula as far as Quebec, that is to say over a distance of 500 miles. I believe there are not more than two drill sheds, while over a similar area there are scores of them in the province of Ontario.
I take the liberty of saying a few words in reference to the expenditure we are making for military purposes in this country. True, I am not an expert in the art of warfare, though my father served as volunteer at the time of the Fenian raids, and though I might have been a warrior myself, had I been bred in a -country where military life constitutes a special! calling.

However, under the Laurier administration, I was engaged in polities in my county, and I took strong exception to the expenditure for military purposes which was increasing at an alarming rate from year to year. At the time the estimates for 1913-14 were voted, on ,May 27th, I sounded a loud note of protest against that extraordinary outlay for militia purposes, and I again utter the same note of warning this year. I showed that the hon. minister in his Main Estimates was asking for $'10,917,305, anjd in his supplementaries, $1,938,905, for the building of drill halls in various localities, etc., making up a total expenditure of $13,196,185.
This year his estimates are not quite so high, though they are yet much too high. We are called upon to vote $10,840,400 on the main estimates, besides $671,000 included in the Estimates of the Department of Public Works, for the building of drill halls, and in the Supplementary Estimates, $741,682, making a total of $12,498,082, which, compared with last year, shows, it is true, a decrease of $684,000.
It must be acknowledged that if the Liberal party had remained in power, we might have had to put up with expenditure even on a larger scale; for the Laurier administration was entering with all sails unfurled into the vortex of militarism. However, I do not propose to be very bitter with the hon. Minister of Militia on that account, for I appreciate his great qualifications as a soldier, and I wish to assure him that he has all my sympathy in the trying task imposed upon him in the country's interest. At the same time, I am a citizen of Canada and the representative of an agricultural county, and my constituents are anxious that I should give expression in this House to their decided views in this connection. I am sincerely of the opinion that fully one-half of the money which we vote for the militia does not reach its proper destination. The annual drill has for its only result the wasteful and useless expenditure of public funds. When the time has come to recruit the required number of men to make up the various companies, the captains or other recruiting officers collect all the loafers, unemployed and drunkards and fill the camp with them. I do not mean that all the .men who go into camp belong to that class, but a goodly number of them do. What military training can they receive during those two weeks in camp, part of which is spent tramping 290
the streets of our cities at night, and getting drunk? Numbers of young men who were leading good lives when they left home, have returned in quite a different disposition. If I had any advice to tender to the hon. Minister of Militia, it would be to revert to the former system which was in vogue thirty or forty years ago, and which may be described as follows:
In every parish there was a captain of the militia, who recruited a company, among people whose ages varied between twenty and forty. It was always the same men who, from year to year, went through the military exercises, generally on Sundays, and they received very little paj for it.
I believe it was not more than fifty cents per day; that was at the time the regular price. If to-day the Government are willing to pay one dollar per day, so much the better, no one surely will object. But those .men were always the same, since they were bound to sign an agreement for three years. During those three years, it goes without saying, that they acquired military training and acquired some experience which turned them into good soldiers.
To-day everything is changed. iSoldiers are enlisted anew every year, and are selected most of the time out of those young men who do not go into camp two years in succession, so that every year a new set of soldiers .are recruited among young men, fifteen, sixteen or eighteen years old at most, who, having nothing else to do in the meantime, enlist and go into camp. As soon as they find a job elsewhere, they leave the camp and never return, so that the whole work has to be begun over again. If the former system to which I referred was reverted to, I think the money would be expended with much more benefit to the country at large.
I do not know whether the suggestion I am about to make is practicable, but it seams to me, from the information I gathered and from my own experience, that the Department of Militia should send every year a certain number of young men taken from the various counties of the Dominion to the military schools, with a view to providing the companies with efficient captains. No doubt the women are induced to be with him in this movement; is he not building places throughout Canada where their choral societies can meet; where they can have tli fir quilting bees and their physical culture classes?
The hon. member for West Lambton this afternoon stated that last year a drill hall was built in the town of Watford and amongst the other activities that developed as the result of the construction of that drill hall, certain societies were formed which held their meetings in this building. I think that it is quite probable that in the progressive town of Watford the good citizens would have their choral societies and their quilting bees if the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence is putting up these buildings throughout Canada; he is providing places where the young women may meet and have their little social entertainments and social gossip at the expense of the people of Canada and thereby the hon. minister is able to claim that he is developing a spirit of militarism among the young women in this country.
The hon. minister stated, that he had also succeeded in enlisting the sympathy of clergymen in the military movement. lected for high military titles. Minister of Militia is proceeding .upon a wrong premises entirely when he states that toy the building of these armouries and the providing of places in small towns where the young men and the young women may congregate during the evenings, he is thereby providing a means of elevating the social and moral dispositions of the young men and women of this country. I deplore the fact that the hon. minister is taking that view. I think that there are other occupations which might be found for the young people of this country besides their being brought together under those military circumstances and their minds being filled with ideas that are not calculated to make them the most practical people in the world.
The hon. minister claims that the farmers are behind him in this military movement. I would say to him that that is not the judgment which I have formed after having given the matter careful consideration One of the great difficulties that we have in this country at the present time is the circumstance that the young men are being drawn away from the farms. Other attractions are growing up in the towns and villages which take away from the old homesteads, and as a consequence the farming communities are peopled largely by the fathers and mothers in homes from which the sons and daughters have departed.
I say that the spirit that the Minister of Militia is developing is calculated more and more to draw our young men away from useful occupations on the farm and elsewhere, and to fill their minds with the notion that there is nothing in this world but a military career for them to follow. What is to become of the farming and other interests of this country if, by reason of the spirit which the minister boasts he is

creating in this country our young men are to be taken away from useful occupations where they can do much more to promote the welfare of this country than by anything they attempt in the military line which the minister prescribes for them? For my part, I feel that the spirit which the minister boasts he is developing does not exist. If there was a time when the minister had the sentiment of the people with him, that time has gone by. There is a limit to everything that is undertaken by individuals, no matter what position in life they may occupy. When they run to extravagance or extremes there will be a reaction with the consequence that the people will get back to sanity, and sanity is very much required in respect to military matters in this country. If we have money to spend, if the Parliament of this country must devote its time to voting supplies, let us vote the money for the important productive industries of this country, and let us have less of this fuss and feathers which the minister has been endeavouring to develop throughout this country during the past three years.

It is
only once a year that members of this House, particularly on this side, have an opportunity of expressing their views of the high and mighty on the treasury benches, and in view of the fact that the Minister of Militia seems to be obsessed with the idea that the military spirit is the great panacea for all the ills that are in this country, it is proper that the time of the House should be taken up in disabusing his mind of some of the notions that seem to possess him. According to the minister, if men were trained for the military as he would have men trained you could do away with schools and churches and reformatories and prisons and asylums and the eleemosynary institutions of the country generally. While the Minister of Militia may have the notion in his head that this military spirit he is developing is making for morality and correct living I venture to say to him with all respect that he is entertaining a false nation in that regard. The

trouble is the minister has so many sycophants and hot air artists telling him what a great man he is. We had illustrations of that to-day. Men would get up and talk about the valour and fearlessness and independent spirit that the minister shows on all occasions, and the wonder is that the minister's head is not turned far more than it is in view of all the flattery he receives. I had occasion a short time ago to look up the word 'paranoia' and the definition of that word which I saw in a medical work describes the disease of the Minister of Militia pretty well. Its characteristics are found in a very highly developed condition in him. You can tell him from morning till night, in season and out of season, that the spirit of militarism which he is seeking to develop does not meet with the approval of the country, and that he is spending altogether too much money on these fads of his, but he still continues to entertain the .same notion and thinks he is in the right. ordinary civil way, he very rarely treats you with the courtesy you would expect from a man occupying his high position. This winter, when proper and jegitimate questions had been placed on the order paper concerning his department, how did he answer them? Many of them in the most contemptuous manner possible. Twelve hundred dollars may not be very much money for the Minister of Militia to throw away, but it is not his money; he is simply a trustee of it for the benefit of the people, and it is just as dishonest for any man who is entrusted with money to give that money to his friends as to apply it to his own purposes. Archibald, for the sole reason that he is a leading Conservative of the town, it is just as dishonest as to apply the money for any other improper purpose. Archibald placed the town in the position that it will be very difficult now for it to get an armoury or drill hall at all, because the minister has a white elephant on his hands now in the shape of this property and he is not likely to buy another property in the town. with the suggestion on the part of his own officers that a suitable lot should be purchased, I cannot understand how he came to ignore these suggestions and to act on the representations of Senator Girroir. Am I not then justified in saying that the idol whom I used to worship has feet of clay, that he is as human as the rest of us, and that he brings politics into the Militia Department, just as the Postmaster General does into his department, and the Lord knows that department is steeped in partisanship. I believe the purchase of this property was an honest mistake on the part of the minister himself; I do not think he looked into the thing, for if he did I do not believe he ever would have recommended the purchase; I believe he was imposed upon.
He is guilty of negligence just the same.

He may be technically culpable, but I do not think there is any moral turpitude on his part in this matter. The minister took the recommendation of the man in charge of the patronage, who was desirous of helping out his political friend Archibald. There is no recommendation from the board of trade or from the town council, and there is no suggestion from anybody that this property should be bought, while at the same time there is absolute condemnation of the property by the minister's own officers. I know from my own personal knowledge that the property is unsuitable for the purpose for which it was purchased. As far as Mr. Archibald personally is concerned I have nothing to say against him. I am glad he made the sale of his property, but when the late Government was in power I protested when I heard that through some manipulation he had arranged for the sale of the property to the Militia Department at $2,500.1 plainly stated to the officers of the Militia Department that if that deal went through it would go through without my acquiescence in it, and I was ready to denounce the thing. I do not desire at all to say anything against Mr. Archibald; I would like to see him get $2,500 for the property if he could, but as the representative of the county I could not justify a steal and a scandal of that kind and I protested against it.

The hon. gentleman
says I have a white elephant on my hands in the shape of this property, and as a matter of fact I did have a white elephant in the shape of an agreement solemnly signed and sealed by my predecessor in office with the owner of this property to pay him $2,500 for it. My hon. friend (Mr. Chisholm) will not deny that. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Chisholm) knows, I refused again and again to pay any such 6um, although application was made again and again by the owner of the property for permission to enter an action to force the department to carry out the Agreement that my predecessor Sir Frederick Borden had entered into to pay $2,500 for this property.
I sent Engineer Bingay, a very excellent officer, and he reported that he had seen the property in bad weather. considered the matter; the thing went on, and, finally, we decided that, as we were paying a very high rent for the property, we would possibly save a good deal of money by buying the property, thus avoiding having to pay rent and the heavy cost of a lawsuit as well. It was, however, the property that had been selected by my predecessor and by the hon. member for the county.

I did not know anything at all about it. As a matter of fact, under the late Government, as far as Antigonish county was concerned, there was no political interference, and the major of the battery did the whole thing. I wish to call the attention of the Minister of Militia to the fact that a few years ago land was chosen in the upper part of Three Rivers for the purpose of holding yearly military training camps.
