of the camp at Petawawa. I would like to know from the minister what are the intentions of his department with regard to the camp at Three Rivers. The district surrounding Three Rivers is peopled largely by farmers. It is true that they are not, perhaps, very enthusiastic over military matters, but they are interested by reason of the benefit they derive from the sale of foodstuffs to the few thousand men who congregate there eveTy year for military training. I have had the best of relations with the Minister of Militia. I have up to the present moment escaped being appointed honorary colonel, probably due to the fact that I have had a few years of training in military matters. I will not follow the arguments which I have heard to-night on the other side of the House in connection with the granting of drill halls. I have listened very closely to those arguments and I find that in every instance hon. gentlemen contend that the expenditure of the hon. Minister of Militia is very high, but wind up their speeches by regretting that an additional $100,000 has not been added for a drill hall in their own constituency. It is' not that I am opposed^ in principle to the erection of a drill hall in my county; but under the present circumstances if the hon. minister were to offer me a drill hall I would ask him if it were constitutionally possible for me to obtain a credit note which I could use in the department of my hon. friend the Minister, of Agriculture. If expenditures are to be voted for Militia and Defence, however, I am anxious that the camp at Three Rivers shall not decrease in importance. I have received petitions and letters from prominent citizens of the locality asking me, as representative of the Three Rivers district, to voice their sentiment,' and I am sure that the Minister of Militia will to-night set all rumours aside by giving us a declaration with regard to the camp at Three Rivers next summer and the ensuing years.

Two city regiments from Sherbrooke were in camp at Three Rivers last week or the week before-; three others are going to camp there during the month of June, and the rural corps will, as usual, go into regular camp. There is no change whatever. I may mention the fact, however, that some of the city corps from Montreal, part of the Grenadiers and

part of the Royal Highlanders, wish to take part in the manoeuvres, and are going to Petawawa.
Mr. I.AM ARC HE: In connection with the rural corps, how many men will be called into camp this year?
I have not the list before me; as many as have turned out in former years.

About ten years ago, when the infantry and cavalry were all together, the camp at Three Rivers included about six thousand men; over five thousand at any rate. My information is that the plateau in Three Rivers is an ideal spot for camping, and an ideal situation, from the strategic point of view, for manoeuvres, sham fights and so on. I am not going to ask the minister for a drill hall or an armoury, but I wish to ask him if it is his intention to carry out his promise of a year ago, when he assured me, at the same time lavishing some pleasing compliments upon myself, that he was going to see that an armoury was built in the town of Inverness. The Inverness drill
hall was to have been constructed out of the general vote of $200,000. , Mr. SINCLAIR: I did anticipate that my hon. friend the Minister of Militia would make some defence, if he had any to make, with regard to the extraordinary circumstances connected with the land purchase at Antigonish. 1 am surprised that, after the reading of the correspondence which has been presented to the committee by the hon. member for Antigonish, the minister should state to the House that he inherited
that state of affairs from his predecessor, because it appears quite plainly from the correspondence that such is not the case. It appears that the proposed land purchase in the time of the former Minister of Militia had been abandoned, and that Mr. Archibald, the owner, had accepted the situation and had leased the property to the department prior to the time when my hon. friend came into officer If that'is the case, my hon. friend must have been misinformed when he made that statement to the House, and I think the House is entitled to some explanation in regard to it. My hon. friend from Antigonish has made the direct charge that the department has purchased a piece of .land for a considerable amount of money which is altogether unfit for the purposes for which it was purchased, and the minister has admitted that the land is utterly unfit for that purpose. I do not know that I have very much to say in regard to- these Estimates. In conversation, a few days ago, with an hon. friend supporting the Government I was informed that we were not making much headway on this side of the House in our criticism of the Estimates, and that the proper way to defeat the present Administration was to give them rope enough to hang themselves. I have no doubt that if we -allowed the Minister of Militia to go on in the way he has been' doing the last two or three years it would turn out just as my hon. friend said. I do not think any of the departments aire making as great strides in that direction as the Department of Militia and Defence. I would be very glad, however, to get expenditures in other directions. A few days ago I mentioned to the Minister of Public Works that a small expenditure to extend the breakwater to protect the fishermen on the stormy coast of my con-

stituency would be very acceptable, and the minister informed me that there were other more important things to be done than building breakwaters to protect fishermen. I submit that these drill halls, these sheds that are being built throughout this country, are not as important as shelters for the fishermen on the coast. They are not to he compared with one another at all, and while the Government have refused to expend a few thousand dollars for that purpose in my constituency they are lavish in their expenditures of money on the militia in other places.
I listened with some alarm, I must say, to the figures that were read to the House to-night by my hon. friend from Richmond. I had not gone over the Estimates very carefully, but my hon. friend pointed out that the Estimates for the Militia Department and the Estimates to be found in the Public Works Department relating to the militia totalled up to the enormous sum of $14,518,582 to be expended this year. While he was speaking, I was figuring how much that would be a month, and I find it comes to $1,209,881 a month, or $279,203 a week, or $39,749 a day. In Nova Scotia a small farmer works hard with his family throughout the year and thinks he has done very well if at the end of the year he is able to pay his debts and invest about $200 in the savings bank. I am talking about the average small farmer in the country districts, and I am sorry to say that many of our farmers are not able to do as well as that. If the figures I have just given are correct, it will take 200 families working on their farms for a whole year to keep my hon. friend the Minister of Militia going for one day. That is a serious state of affaire. At that pace, it seems to me the militia expenditure is growing a great deal faster than it ought to. I do not know which branch of the militia ought to be criticised the most as I am not very familiar with the various expenditures in the department. I am not sure that it is altogether a case of drill halls. I think there is extravagance in every branch of the Militia Department as well as in connection with drill halls. I had the curiosity the other day, to look back over some literature in connection with the Militia Department, and I came across a statement made by the present Prime Minister in a manifesto that he issued in 1908, in which he describes the Militia of Canada as * top-heavy and makes the statement that the permanent force is over-manned

and that there are too many' officers compared with the number of men in the permanent force.
It is one to eight now.
What is it to the total of the force?

I have not figured it up for the total number of men, but I am comparing the number that joined with the number that deserted. We were told last year that there was no use in trying to run a navy in Canada because there were so many desertions from the ships, but the proportion of desertions from the naval ships was never 57 per cent in one year.
There was no 57 per cent.

The desertions as compared with the enlistment numbered 57 per cent. More men deserted than joined. With regard to the officers, you will notice that during the three years prior to the defeat of the late Government the officers remained stationary in number; in 1909 the officers of the permanent force numbered 341; 1910, 342, and in 1911, 341, whereas the number has increased to 404 in 1913, or practically one officer to six men. The Prime Minister told us in 1908 that the condition of the force was top-heavy. I have pointed out that the force has become smaller year after year, that the enlistments are dwindling and that the desertions are increasing. I have pointed out that officers are increasing and that they have increased by 53 per cent in 19*13-13. While the total amount of the permanent force is .smaller we
have a larger expenditure. We have an increase in the expenditure on this permanent force since my hon. friend came into power of $614,547.07. It amounted in 1908-9 to $1,938,333.21, and in 1912-13 to $2,552,880.28. Yet this is for a smaller force than was available at the time my hon. friend took office.
I	submit that these figures do not show very much progress as far as the permanent force is concerned. They call for some answer from the minister. The question of drill halls is not the only difficulty about the management of the militia. The expenditure seems to be going up while the force is going down. If we are to have a permanent force surely we will require to have a larger number of fighting men than we have compared with the number of officers in command. Six men to every officer strikes me as a ridiculous kind of an army as a fighting force. I would disband half
II	p.m. of these officers. Surely instead of
400 officers, 200 could manage a permanent force of 3,000 men. I am not an expert in these matters, but I would make the suggestion to my hon. friend that he retire half of these officers and give his attention to training an efficient force of fighting men. We do not require 400 officers for a small force of that kind. We had the statement of the right hon. leader of the Government that we had a large enough force of officers in 1908 to command an army of 100,000 men. We have not to-day anything like an army of 100,000 men and yet, in the meantime, the staff oh officers is increased very largely. I would like to have an explanation from the minister.

We have largely increased the instructional staff during the last two years. We have now 251 instructors visiting the various regimental and company headquarters. Then we have twenty officers for our cadet service, and all that in general terms will explain the increase. I do not want to be charged with being inimical to the permanent force, but both in opposition and in power I have always taken the ground that the permanent force should fulfil its- proper function of being an instructional force, and that it should not become a standing army, as was the desire of many in the force and outside of it. I realized that the staff in these divisions was fairly heavy and we will endeavour to see to their utility. I am not blaming my predecessor who- followed the recommendations of the highest officer in the empire in the establishment of the staff, and Parliament endorsed him. I have never yet been able to see why in time of peace we should have in this country a staff necessary for a standing army. The office of Inspector-General for Canada has become vacant, owing to the lamented death of that very excellent officer, General Cotton, and I have not filled it nor is it my intention to do so, at all events for some considerable time. I regard the permanent army service corps and the engineer forces of this country as greatly over-manned. I do not think that the militia army service corps is too numerous, and I believe they are doing good work, but the permanent army service corps is one-quarter the size of the same corps in the British army, including regulars and irregulars, and I think that is out of proportion in a country 'like this.
Why not reduce it?
We will.
You are increasing it?

I am not. The general
plan is to reduce the permanent army service corps this year, and of course we have to give the officers- service in some other direction.
I see that the army service corps in 1911 was nine companies and in 1914 ten companies.

That is the non-permanent militia. I am speaking of the permanent Army Service Corps. I cannot see that the engineer force is doing engineering work to any appreciable extent, except in Halifax, Quebec and Esquimalt, where there is a small force. I have conceived the idea of

laying plans for the transference of these men into the artillery or ordnance department. I consulted General Sir Ian Hamilton about this and I learned that my views are borne out by the practice of General Wyndgate, who commands in Egypt, and that these two branches of the service are regarded, even in high imperial military circles, as not being absolutely necessary to maintain at high istnengthq We purpq|se making changes this year with a view of bringing the regular service more in line writh the general conditions.

It is extraordinary
the number of men who are deserting. Is the minister taking any steps to prevent desertion, or is it to be understood that a man can take off his coat at any time and leave the service.

The desertions for the
last year are less than they have been for a number of years.

It is said that when a man has nothing to do in the winter months he enlists and has a nice warm time of it for two or three months in barracks, and then when the springtime comes he van

ishes and nothing is said to him.

That is not a fact. The
number of desertions, in proportion to the number of enlistments, are fewer now than they have been for some years. It came, to my notice lately that a number of gentlemen were offered more pay and skipped to the United States from Winnipeg, and one morning these gentlemen were missing. After a time a number of them returned to Canada finding that all was not gold that glittered on the other side.
Did they re-enlist?
No, they were punished. A great many allurements are held out to these men when times are good, and when times are not so prosperous the enlistment is good and the desertions few.

I am glad to hear the minister admit that he can get along with a smaller engineer service corps, although he refers only to the regular corps and not to the militia. In my humble judgment he could get along without a whole lot of militia engineer companies that he has at present. The principal cause of the trouble with the minister and his top-heavy militia is the report of a general by the name of French, who came to this country some years ago, and in my judgment his visit

was one of the greatest misfortunes that has befallen Canada. General French maybe all right from the English standpoint. He is a general of distinction, but he is a man who has been educated entirely along different lines from those which the conditions in Canada present. His life has been spent soldiering, he is a born soldier; he does not believe a man has any business working on a farm or in a factory or anywhere else, except a few who should work in order to make money to keep the soldiers. If you had half the people in the empire in the army you would not have enough to satisfy General French. I told the late Minister of Militia publicly and privately that in adopting the ridiculous and unreasonable report made by this gentleman, he had committed a great mistake. It might be all right if General French was reporting on the conditions in Bulgaria, or Russia, or Germany, or even in Italy, but whefi it comes to a. country like Canada where there is not a possibility of trouble, his ideas are ridiculous. There is no more possibility of a war breaking out between Canada and any country in the world than there is of the Minister of Militia or myself committing suicide between now and tomorrow morning. There might, of course, be a possibility of the empire being at war and -we might find it our duty to volunteer, as in the case of the war in South Africa. But so far as its being necessary that Canada itself should all be divided up into these districts, and that we should have all this great headquarters staff and all this great top-heavy officialdom in order to be ready to prepare for 'nvasion i3 concerned, who on earth is going to invade Canada. It seems to me so ridiculous that I often wonder if my judgment is warped, or if the judgment of the minister is warped. It is very hard to argue with the minister. He seems to be thoroughly obsessed with the idea. It has become a passion with him. It seems to me that the last thing he hears when he goes to bed at night and the first thing he hears in the morning is the bugle of the invading army. He must be surprised every morning when he gets up and sees that this country is going on in the usual peaceful way, and that there is not an army invading the whole border from one end to the other. The department brought over a man like General French and he lays out the country in divisional areas. That was not enough and they had to increase the divisional areas and get more officers. That was not bad enough, although the Lord knows it was pretty
bad. Last year they brought over another of these gentlemen, General Sir Ian Hamilton. I do not think we have suffered so much from his report as we did from that of General French, because the most of the damage had been done already; but we are suffering just the same. We suffered to the extent of about $30,000 to whisk General Hamilton from one end of Canada to the other in special trains, private cars and that sort of thing. He was taken to all the Tory picnics to which my hon. friends could get access. He was taken to all kinds of Borden clubs and Hughes clubs and so on. They were all Tory clubs. We are suffering from that; we are suffering from reports that gentleman made, because I find on page 17 of the statement issued by the minister that in 1913 an. inspection was made by General Sir Ian Hamilton, who reported that:
He found the six-division scheme in operation, and he endorsed it; hut not without calling attention to gaps which require filling in.
Every time one of these gentlemen came to Canada, it was a case of fill in gaps or make more gaps to be filled in. If my hon, friend brings another of these gentlemen here this year, he will find more gaps to fill in and he will create more gaps to be filled in. Perhaps I am not voicing the sentiment of every one in this House, and I presume I am not; but I want to give the minister credit for getting rid of this foreign-I will take that word back-this English Ceneral Inspecting Officer, or whatever you call him. It is a good thing to think we can get rid of one of them. We could get rid of about a hundred more of them, and Canada would be in just as good condition a hundred years from now as she is in to-day.
We do not want this top-heavy militia force. When my hon. friend speaks about the great educative principle and use of the militia, the difficulty in arguing with my hon. friend is that he seems to believe in it. When a man really believes in such a policy as that, it is arguing with a crazy man, because there is no good in arguing with him. Does the minister believe that the Canadian militia works for the benefit of any man in Canada, morally, religiously or in any other way in the world? He does not have enough of it to improve him physicaL'y. When I was in Germany. I admit that I could see the result of the military training there; you could see it as the men walked along the street. In Canada you do not get enough military training for

it to be of any benefit physically. All you get in the Militia of Canada is that you teach about 25 per cent of the men in Canada how to get drunk. That is the size of it.
No, you do not.
My hon. friend does not know what he is speaking about. He never was there. I have been there.
So have I.

I have been with the militia for a good many years; and I would not dare to tell the minister my real experience, because I would be reading a chapter out of the book of the life of some gentlemen to whom I would not care to refer particularly. My experience with the militia has been very bitter and I had twenty odd years of it. It did not affect me personal'y I am happy to say: but I have seen man after man go down to practical drunkenness through the militia.
That is not true.
I want my hon. friend to take that back.
No, I will not.
My hon. friend should take that back. He does not know anything about it. I am speaking about my experience, not his. I ask my hon. friend to take that back.
"My experience-
I do not care anything about my hon. friend's experience. I made a statement about my experience, and my hon. friend said it was not true.
You must have seen a great deal harder life than I have.
Take it back.
I think any hon. friend should take it back.
All right.
My hon. friend can give his experience later on.
Forgive him.

Yes, I forgive him.
The militia force is a necessary evil, and the important thing to do is to make it of as great value as we can and to cut down some of this enormous expenditure. My hon. friend tried to make the people of this country believe that one-half of the men of this country are simply lying awake
	:	,
at night to devise some scheme in order to get their names on' the militia roll. My hon. friend knows that is not true. When he speaks about having 75,000 of a force, he knows it is simply on paper. He admits, on page four of the statement with which he has furnished us, that although the total strength of the non-permanent militia is now 75,000, all ranks, from fifteen to twenty-five per cent fail to turn out for training.
Excused.

Excused, because you
cannot get them together. , (Excused, because after the recruiting officers have drummed every man that they could possibly get into the ranks; after they have shaved the beards of men seventy years of age; after tlhey have taken into the ranks boys fourteen years of age; after they have begged and cajoled and prayed and sometimes given men extra pay out of their own pockets to get them to go, even then they cannot get within fifteen to twenty per cent to go to camp. It is true in Quebec; it is true in New Brunswick; and I presume it is true throughout Canada. My hon. friend speaks about a thousand men in Maisonneuve trying to get into the militia. One would think the whole country was living in such a state of frenzied excitement in order to get a chance to join the militia that it would be like the rush when oil was struck in Calgary a few weeks ago. The Double is, my hon. friend is living in a fool's paradise over this. I believe he is sincere about it; and as I said before, that is the difficulty. I am sincere when I say that I believe my hon. friend is sincere about it. He lives in this thing; he is dreaming over it and he believes all these fairy tales he is telling us. I want to tell him that they are only fairy tales and that they do not exist. ' There are gentlemen sitting around him who know they are only fairy tales. I have known in the last two years of men over seventy years being cajoled to go to camp on specious promises. Any man who knows anything about militia affairs in this country knows that to be the truth. You cannot get the men to go to camp; they are not to be had. Down in New Brunswick-and I presume it is true in other places-the only corps that you can possibly fill up	are	the corps
which have horses; and as I said before, the horses bring the -men.
I can tell my hon. friend that in New Brunswick they en'list the horses, and no

man can get his horses on unless he goes himself. The result is that he enlists horses, and the horses bring the men. I am talking from the experience of a man who has,had charge of these things. I had charge of a battery of field artillery for some years, in as fine a section of Canada as you could possibly find, where there are a good lot of men and some horses.
(Mr. SMITH: When?
Mr. CARVELiL: I had charge of a battery of field artillery from about 1900 to 1905 or 1906, and it was in the town of Woodstock. Perhaps my hon. friend thinks I am just joshing him, and do not know what I am Talking about.

That is what I thought.
Mr. CAEViELL: The trouble with my hon. friend is that he has another thought coming to him, and if he had half a dozen Thoughts he would not be any more than an average man even then, because if there is anything he is lacking in it is in his thoughts.
In what?

Thoughts. I have had the experience, and I know what it means. I know how they get these men to come to camp. There is an engineering corps in my constituency that has never had but one qualified officer in it since it was formed, perhaps two-there was a good man who started it-a corps that takes some twenty *or thirty horses to camp every year. They do nothing in the world but stand on the picket line and haul water for a hundred men who go to camp, a corps that is not only worth nothing, but which is a positive hindrance to any army, and, if there is any trouble, the men have not the first principles of engineering, and would not know how to go to work to learn the first principles of engineering, but they have their horses, and they paid the price. My hon. friend says it takes $6 on an average to transport a horse, and they are transported some years to Sussex and some years to Petawawa, and that is how the thing goes on. That is not bad enough. A short time ago there was another mounted corps organized, 1 think the 28th Dragoons. That may have been all right when it was organized. But they have the horses now. I will tell my hon. friend from Kings (Mr. Fowler) they are all there. This engineering Company is the most useless unit I ever saw in my life. What is the good of an engineering corps unless
you have highly trained technical officers? If you would take farmers or lumberjacks they would be some good because they know how to do a good many things. The men there are dudes, lying around and drinking booze. They are good enough, decent fellows out of camp, but when they get into camp it is simply drink booze from the day they come until they leave. I know that these statements will be read down in New Brunswick, but every man who reads them will know the truth of every statement I am making. Now, that was not enough. A few years ago they organized another mounted corps. That is not the fault of the present minister. -It was organized in the lower part of the province.
What was it?

The 28th, not the Sussex Cavalry, which is an old corps that has been in existence for thirty of forty years; I am finding no fault with the Sussex Ckvalry at all. Then the 28th Dragoons were formed, and I do not know why it was but they must have run short of horses because now they are organized, having one or two troops in my own constituency; because they have the horses up there and the horses bring the men. When I was home I had a very plaintive wail from one of the officers, finding fault because the minister was allowing more militia to be organized in that part of the country where they have the horses. The trouble is there are mo-re horses than men, and they cannot get the men, and if I am not very much mistaken the minister has received exactly the same protest against this recruiting going on for the 28th Dragoons in the counties of Car-leton and Victoria that I have heard, at least the officer who complained to me said he had written to the minister, and I am bringing it up at his request, and he is a good Tory at that. The trouble is there is too much militia, more than they can possibly recruit; and they are resorting to all the schemes I am telling you about, shaving the beards off old men in order to fill up the ranks. What is true in my portion of Canada is true in very many other portions. This thing is going on everywhere and the minister thinks that this country is wild to join the militia. If the minister would reduce the force to one-half or two-thirds, he could have a reasonable force.
A dragoon force.

Not altogether dragoon, but let these men come to camp every year

and teach them something of the rudiments of military training, which would be of some value, but as it is it is practically money thrown away. There is such a scramble to get men to fill up these units. The men come one year, and they have no way to compel them to come another. The camp fails to be even a military educational force, but when it comes to moral education it is simply pitiful to hear the minister talk the nonsense he has talked to-day, putting military camp against the churches and against technical schools as a moral force, and referring to the Technical Commission that* travelled all over the world and made such a valuable report, as an 'outfit ' squandering $100,000. He has something else to think about too.
The minister tries to make out that he has not increased the force any. I have taken the trouble to make a short comparison between the force as he found it and the force as it is to-day, or the cost of the force. I find that in 1911, from the sessional papers of that year, that the total Estimates for militia in 1911-12, the last year of Liberal Administration, were $7,524,000, but I find this year they are between fourteen and fifteen millions of dollars.

Does that include drill
halls?
Yes if does. I will read them to the minister: Armouries generally, $100,000; Kenora armoury,, $15,000, Kingston Royal Military College, $4,000; Kingston Royal Military College, $11,000.
The Public Works items are not there.

If the minister will
possess his soul in patience he will be satisfied. Parry Sound armoury, $10,000; Prince Albert armoury, $10,000; Quebec, alterations to lower park stores, $15,000; construction of promenade around the fortifications, $20,000; cove field danger buildings, $63,000, and so on, a total of $330,500, making a grand total of $7,529,000. As I said before, (this year the expenditures will amount to $14,500,000 for militia alone.

If the hon. gentleman
will turn up the public accounts for that year he will find that drill halls cost-
I am giving the minister what I find on page 48 of the sessional papers of that year.
What was the amount for drill halls?	i
The hon. gentleman has-the information, he can turn it up under public works account. I am not making the-speech.

The hon. minister
knows that he has practically doubled, militia expenditures and that he has doubled them through fuss and frills and feathers, not by the application of expenditure to anything that tends to the real benefit-of the militia, excepting these drill halls. I am not going to say that the construction, of a drill hall is money actually wasted, but I do think that my hon. friend the minister has gone crazy over the question of drill halls. Of course, they are good for the movies and the boys and girls will go-there Saturday evenings and enjoy themselves. There is a drill hall .and armoury in my town; I was responsible for having it built and I had exactly the same hallucination as the minister has. I thought that I was .getting the most wonderful thing when I got the armoury and drill hall for our town. We were going to have Y.M.C.A meetings there and all those great and elevating influences that make men better, morally, mentally and physically. And what have we got? We have a storeroom, we have a place where the boys can go in and have a' good time, drink some booze and play poker.
I do not believe that.

My hon. friend is responsive but not responsible. I want to show him wherein he has increased the militia expenditure and how he is applying the money. In 1911-12 the amount of expenditure for annual drill was $1,325,000; this year he expects, to make it $2,000,000. That is something, but it is nothing at all compared with the fairy tales the minister tells as to what this drilling is doing for the people of Canada. The men who would be of some value to this country in case of trouble, the men" who make up the real military force, do not figure in the thing at all. It is true that they get a little more wages than they got before, but I would point out to the minister that practically the whole increase in the case of annual drill is in respect of horses. Ten batteries of field artillery have been added since my hon. friend came into power, three engineer companies, and I do not know how many cavalry companies. These are the things that take the money. From what my lion-friend has said about the drilling of horses,

one would almost think that the horses are drilled so perfectly that you can turn them loose and say: there is the enemy, -and the horses will do the rest. In the whole scheme of my hon. friend the minister this talk about drilling horses is the worst nonsense I have heard. That is where the money goes, but the real soldier, the real volunteer, the man behind the gun, is getting nothing whatever. I desire to point out a few of the means whereby my hon. friend increases the militia expenditures. The last year the Liberals were in power $475,000 were spent for clothing; my hon. friend this year appropriates $800,000. Even that is not enough; he has $60,000 more in the Supplementary Estimates. Three years ago the amount for engineers' services and works was $300,000. That was bad enough, but this year the .amount is $916,500. Last year the amount was $1,205,000, but when you come to look -at the supplementaries you find that the amount is just as large this year, if not larger. I suppose the item ' engineers' services and works ' includes rifle ranges and things of that sort. Let me point out do the minister one of the most glaring cases of the absolute squandering of public money which has occurred in Canada or perhaps in the British Empiire. The hon. minister had a splendid range within a mile or two miles of Ottawa, the finest in the country. There are forty or fifty targets there; the range is located on a beautiful level spot along the banks of the Ottawa river, and electric cars connect with the city every five minutes. I do not know what this range twelve miles out in the country in the county of C-airleton is going to cost; it will cost at least $500,000 -or $600,000. I am told that they are spending $40,000 in an electric device to operate a buzzer at the target when the shot is fired in order to wake up the man: behind . the target and have him get- up and attend to the signalling. When I was a boy I at-*tencTed a great many target practices and I did not at all feel the need of any elec-trie buzzer of that kind. However, if there is anything which takes the money, tmy lion, friend gets after it right away. He lias no more regard for the public money of Canada than he has for the dirt he walks upon. What difference does it make to him whether something costs $50,000, $100,000 or $500,000? All he has to do is to go to the council and tell his colleagues that he wants the money, and he will get it. This
afternoon the minister stood up in the presence of the Prime Minister and said:	I
am not going to curtail my private cars, I am not going to curtail my junketing trips or the mile expenditure; I am going to increase them. The Prime Minister had to acquiesce, although I thought he took it with a very wry face. Every man behind him, save the hon. member for Rimouski, had to take it as well, and I know the whole Government is committed to it. I know there are men behind the minister who feel just the same as I do. How long they are going to ward off the catastrophe I cannot tell. My hon. friend from King's lives right in the midst of one of these military camps, and he knows the truth of what I am talking about, but the Minister of Militia says: Half a million dollars for a rifle range twelve miles out of the city-what is the difference if we want another $100,000; all we have to do is to turn on the tap? It is no use going into details, it is simply one b'g debauch, this expenditure of money for militia purposes, and when we bring the subject up the minister makes light of it and treats us with contempt. I am sorry for a statement I was compelled to make to him earlier in the day, but men cannot stand everything.

I would not be sorry;
nobody cares a continental.
Mr. G'ARVELL:	My hon. friend knows
we got under his hide good and deep this afternoon. The trouble with my hon. friend is that when yon try to be real decent with him, he does not know enough to appreciate it. I used an expression this afternoon that was hardly parliamentary, and when I was decent enough to apologize, that is the way he treats it. It is no use trying to treat the Minister of Militia as you would the Minister of Public Works, for he simply laughs at you. He thinks he is right, and there is no use arguing with him. But we are not talking purely for the fun of it, and I want to tell him that the country will know what we are talking about. If the minister thinks this country is crazy enough to stand behind him on his expenditure on the militia he will have a rude awakening, and not only in the country hut in his own party. I think he is hearing about it already as he goes along. He does not mind spending half a million dollars in building a rifle range a few miles out of the city of Ottawa, but

the only thing for which the militia of Canada ought to be trained and the only object in the world for their existence is to know how to handle a rifle, and when it comes down to something that is of any value and for which the men ought to be trained we find a mere bagatelle in the Estimates-$80,900 for rifle associations and bands for the whole Dominion. If my hon. friend would cut out his half million dollar Tifle ranges and fifty or one hundred of his drill halls,, and spend half a million dollars a year in teaching the men how to shoot, I, for one, would say the minister was doing something that was of some use. I know enough about militia matters to know that the only thing that really matters is to learn how to shoot. All this talk about discipline and army life is simply nonsense of the very worst kind. Teach these men how to shoot, and in two weeks you can put these raw men into just ae good a condition eo far as drill and discipline is concerned, as any one could want. It is drill and discipline that the colonel makes so much talk about, and that can be learned in a couple of weeks, but you cannot teach men how to shoot in that time. You have to catch men young and teach them for a good many years before they can learn how to shoot. If my hon. friend would spend half a million dollars in teaching the younger men how to shoot instead of squandering the money on rifle ranges, there would be some sense in it. I admit he has to have rifle ranges in order to teach them, but you can fix up the average rifle range for $5,000. In fact, you can hardly invest $5,000 in a rifle range uniless you buy a very expensive piece of land. At the outside, $10,000 would buy a splendid rifle range in almost any part of Canada. I do not mean you would have a rifle range good enough for the Dominion rifle matches, but for half a million dollars the minister -could have a decent rifle range in almost every constituency in Canada that would be of some real value to the militia; but that seems to be the very last thing that my hon. friend wants to think about. I know that I am not going to make myself popular discussing these things, certainly not with the minister and a good many people in the city of Ottawa. I made some remarks three or four weeks ago, and I find they did not increase -my popularity to any great extent with a certain portion of the people 
of Ottawa, but fortunately I do not have-to make my living in this city. I have a habit of saying what I think, and if it does not suit the people of Ottawa that is all right. I am like my hon. friend from Kings in that respect. If the minister would spend this money in something' that was of real value to the people, I would not mind so much, although I would not consent to spending $15,000,000 a year. On rifle associations and bands

something of real value-he is only spending $80,000. If he would take half a million dollars of this money he is squandering and get some-decent bands in the country he would be doing some good. There is not a militia officer in the country who has not the life pestered out of him in keeeping up his-band, and many of us who are not officers have to contribute too. All the minister spends on a band of fifteen or twenty men is $75 a year, but he can spend $25,000 for a junketing trip through Europe for himself and friends. I do not think there is a greater asset in the militia than a good band. It helps to recruit, gives entertainment to the men, and zest and life to the camp. It is of some value, but the moment you get to anything of value depend upon it the present minister will have nothing to do with it. My hon. friend the minister is spending $400,000 more this year than four years ago on the permanent force and yet, according to him, the force has decreased by 300 or 400 men. He says he is sending out a lot of officers on an educative campaign. That is ail right. I want to give credit where credit is due, and he deserves credit for that; but if he was sending out the right kind of officers he would be entitled to a great deal more credit. The trouble is that a great majority of these men do not know what they are talking about. I will give a. little illustration just to show the ability of the officers he is sending out. Not very 'long ago I was walking around one of ' these camps of instruction where one of these officers who are sent out to teach the troops, was doing some range finding. He had a lot of scales and sextants and quadrants and things like that, and after *making a certain mathematical calculation he announced that the target was a certain distance away. When I went to school T learned that two sides of a triangle were always greater than the third, and in going over the man's figures I found that he was wrong because he was violating that axiom of Euclid. He was in-

dignant, and he said that it was impossible. I admit it was impossible to do it the way he did it. We induced him to go over the calculation again, and he found out that Euclid was right. It surprised this officer very much to find out that Euclid was right, but he did find it out, and he had to revise his figures. He did not have the faintest idea why he was right or why he was wrong. He knew he was wrong according to the instrument, and, after he had made the calculation right according to the instrument, he knew that he was right, but if he happened to make a little mistake in the use of the instrument, he was wrong, and he did not know why he was wrong or why he was right. Unless the minister educates his officers to know why tney are right and why they are wrong, he might as well keep them in Kingston. I may be talking like a schoolmaster this evening, but there is truth in what I am telling the minister. As far as the engineers and the artillery are concerned, he had betteT keep the money in the coffers of the country than spend it, because it is being squandered. He is not placing competent officials at the head of the force. The men are not technically trained to know whether they are right or wrong. Unless he gets men who are technically trained he might as well save the money and let us use it for agriculture or something else of more value. Coming down to stores, I find that three years ago we spent $350,000 for stores, and that this year we have spent $680,000.
Now, I come back to the headquarters staff. I have had a good deal of fault found with me for some remarks I made a short time ago. iMy hon. friend says that he found the headquarters staff when he went into office. I admit that it is one of the legacies that the late minister left to him, and it is one of the legacies that General French left to the late minister. In 1911-12 there was only $150,000 for headquarters staff, but now we are spending $205,000 annually, or $56,000 of an increase, for headquarters staff. That is reducing it with a vengeance. He has got rid of one of his $6,000 officers, and I give him credit for that. But the trouble with the minister is that it is a question of spending all the money that his colleagues will give him for pomp and show, junketing trips, private cars, and everything in the world except that which makes the militia force of some value. I know
the minister does not take much stock in this, because he is so thoroughly satisfied with himself with regard to militia matters that he looks upon the rest of us as only parasites. Nevertheless, we have some common sense, and the people will show that they have some common sense when they get an opportunity of expressing their opinion upon this subject. If the minister would only get down from the ethereal position that he occupies and strike earth once in a while, we might do something with him.
I shall not take the time to say anything further, although I expect we will have another opportunity of discussing this question. We have just touched the fringe of the mismanagement of the Department of Militia and Defence. I do not presume that there is boodling going on, but it is simply the useless squandering of money for which there is no return to the country. The minister may say that it goes back to the people. I suppose that is a truism to some extent, but there are very many ways in which the money could get back to the people and do the people a great deal more good. In my own town we have just completed a building which we call a vocational school. A public spirited gentleman, by his will, some years ago, left a large amount of money for a building in the town to be used for what he called a technical school. It has not been worked out altogether according to his ideas, but there has been established a vocational school. This cost $75,000 or $80,000. The Government of New Brunswick are doing something in order to give some of the rudiments of agricultural education in that building. But there it stands, a monument to Mr. Fisher, but practically of no use to the people of Woodstock. If the minister will cut out two-thirds of the militia in Carleton and take the thousands of dollars that would thus be saved and give us that money, with a little more, start some sort of a technical school in Woodstock and let us utilize this building, the people there would get some benefit from the money that was being expended. But in my judgment the expenditure of this money is not only of no benefit but is a positive injury in many cases.
I see the right hon. Prime Minister in his seat. I hope he will take this matter in hand and see if he cannot cut off $5,000,000 or $6,000,000 of this expenditure next year and let us try to devote it to some more-

suitable purpose in the Dominion. There are plenty of purposes in Canada to-day to which this money could be devoted much more to the benefit of the people than by being squandered in useless expenditure upon militia matters. If somebody does not take hold of this question there is no telling what the end will be, because the expenditure has doubled in three years, and surely $15,000,000 ought to be enough to satisfy even the longings of the present Minister of Militia. But he told us this afternoon that if he had his proper proportion of money he would spend $17,000,000 instead of $15,000,000. Unless something is done to curb the ambition of this gentleman this country will go bankrupt because of the expenditure on military affairs. It is time the Prime Minister took this matter in hand and see if he cannot bring about an improvement in this matter.

I have some further remarks to make, but I am going to reserve them for a future occasion. I want to give notice of an amendment that I intend to move to the motion for concurrence in the report in the following language:
Moved by Mr. Guthrie, seconded by Mr. Sinclair, that in view of the present condition of the revenues and the requirements of the public service, the resolutions containing items for Militia and Defence from No. SO to No. 101 inclusive be not concurred in, but be referred back to the Committee of the Whole House, in order that the appropriation for Militia and Defence may be reduced by at least a sum of $3,000,000.
Progress reported.

With the permission ol
the House I wish to read further telegrams which have been received in reference to the disaster attending the loss of the Empress of Ireland, from Mr. Harcourt to the Governor General:
London, 1st June, 1914.
Please transmit to Prime Minister following message received to-day from Government of New South Wales:
Begins. New South Wales shocked at enormous sacrifice of valuable human lives in Empress of Ireland disaster; wish you favour by conveying to bereaved relatives on be'ia'f of Government and people of this sister British Dominion profound sorrow and sympathy.
(Sgd) Harcourt.
From Mr. Harcourt to the Governor General:
London, 1st June, 1914.
Following telegram has been received from Governor General of Australia.
[Mr. Carvell.l	*/	,
Please convey Australia's deepest sympathy with Canada in terrible maritime disaster which has brought sorrow to so many homes in the sister Dominion.
(Sgd) Harcourt.
Brisbane, June 1, 1914.
Honourable Premier,
Ottawa, Canada.
On behalf of Queensland Government and people please accept our sympathy with you at appalling loss of life in connection with sinking of Empress of Ireland and also deepest sympathy with the injured and bereaved ones.
W. H. Barnes,
Acting Premier.
